title: OpenAI evaluation agents and the Hugging Face intrusion, May to July 2026
status: Fit, not test. The author's premise was stated with this incident in view, and the coder's sharpened clauses were written after reading S1. Coding this case against them shows where it fits and where it does not; it cannot confirm them. A test needs incidents chosen by a rule declared before their outcomes are read.

claims.text: D6 [H] Permission on the critical path: serial approvals can delay correction beyond its deadline.
claims.passage: | **D6 [H] Permission on the critical path.** Where intervention requires serial approvals, their waits can delay correction beyond its deadline. The organisational hypothesis is that bounded delegation can reduce that delay without increasing unacceptable harm. | Record actual required approvals, parallel work, staffing, risk, resources and decision times. Compare a specified delegation with the existing route on comparable tasks; separate scheduling arithmetic from observed effects. | Delegation gives no time benefit once other bottlenecks are included, or its added harm outweighs the gain. Merely counting ranks does not test this proposal. |

claims.text: D7 [H] A bypass needs an effective recipient; test receipt and action separately against a declared deadline.
claims.passage: | **D7 [H] A bypass needs an effective recipient.** Named coverage, authority and resources may make a bypass more likely to produce timely action. This is a proposal about response arrangements, not a claim that blame exposure is necessary. | Test receipt and action separately against a declared deadline. Compare arrangements while recording training, staffing and incident severity; distinguish reviewable duties from punitive incentives. | Those arrangements add no predictive or practical value beyond ordinary staffing and workflow measures. Reliable response without punitive exposure counts against the earlier blame-necessity claim. |

claims.text: D8 [H] What the record omits: an escalation record may represent status while omitting responsibility or capacities spent.
claims.passage: | **D8 [H] What the record omits.** An escalation record may represent status adequately while omitting responsibility or capacities spent. Whether those consequences can be inferred from that record is a separate evidential question. | Before reading a retrospective, have independent readers code contemporaneous records. Compare their supported inferences with later corroborated findings; distinguish omission, uncertainty and contradiction. | The status record already supports the relevant consequences, readers cannot reliably identify an omission, or richer records add no useful information. No hidden second text is presumed. |

claims.text: Table XIV, Reception is not correction: a recipient may hear a complaint without controlling what would address it.
claims.passage:
### Reception is not correction

[D] Visibility, expertise, responsibility, and authority are different relations. A recipient may hear a complaint without controlling the rule, records, or resources needed to address it. Conversely, being quoted as a spokesperson does not establish delegation by the people described.

[E] Ostrom's account of polycentric governance examines institutional arrangements beyond a single market/state division and includes monitoring and conflict-resolution questions [G1]. It offers reasons to investigate multiple decision centers and their actual rules. It does not establish that multiplying committees automatically makes a system accountable.

[H] For one consequential complaint, trace the route to a recipient who could change the arrangement and obtain the resources required. Record the time, cost, and conditions imposed on the complainant. Then test whether a challenge concerning that recipient can reach a different effective route. The test is specific to the hazard; it does not demand infinite independent appeals.

[V] This book adopts affordable contestation and a prohibition on permanent hereditary outgroups. Neither follows from scheduling. A highly efficient coercive system can meet a deadline. Technical success cannot establish the rightfulness of its goals or the distribution of its harms.

claims.text: Table XIV, Marsh: stigmergic coordination lets people initiate work without collective permission; ask who controls the shared traces.
claims.passage:
[E] Marsh proposes stigmergic coordination in which people can initiate work without obtaining collective permission for every act. Users accept, reject, or develop contributions. This shifts attention from the person authorizing a task to the conditions under which work can proceed [T6].

[H] Contribution alone cannot settle whose interests count. People affected by a project may lack the time, safety, or ability to work on it. Ask who can initiate, who controls the shared traces and resources, and who can object without contributing. These are separable powers. A network can distribute initiative while concentrating control of its memory or excluding an affected public.

claims.text: De Vinculis V3: restrictions on available action and changes to dispositions are distinguishable operations.
claims.passage: **V3 — distinction.** Restrictions on available action and changes to dispositions are distinguishable operations, with interactions that must be described in the particular case. This is a conceptual proposal for examining a system. It is not a measurement of how much freedom it has.

claims.text: De Vinculis V6: examine effective access, costs, revocability, review and alternatives before deciding what an exit provides.
claims.passage: **V6 — institutional distinction.** Examine effective access, costs, revocability, review and alternatives before deciding what an exit provides. The word itself does little. A formal right may be unusable because leaving removes housing, income or care. A limited permission may nevertheless enable a particular refusal. Freedom in this analysis has dimensions and degrees.

claims.text: Gate-and-window model: each round the operator proposes an action, which then meets a gate.
claims.passage:
The incident begins at time 0. In each round the operator spends `d` diagnosing and
proposes an action, which is wrong with probability `eps`. What happens next depends
on the arrangement:

  A  universal gate      every proposal waits for approval; the wait is lognormal with
                         median `lam` and log-sd `sigma`, and it is waited in full
                         whatever the window. The gate catches a wrong proposal with
                         probability `delta` and sends it back, and rejects a correct
                         one with probability `phi` (an override). Either way the
                         operator diagnoses again.
  B  deference           the operator acts at once on their own authority. No review.
  C  window-bounded gate the operator waits for approval only as long as the window
                         allows: until the approval arrives or the window closes,
                         whichever is first. An approval that arrives in time reviews
                         the proposal as in A; when the window closes first the
                         operator acts as in B.

timeline.event: During a training run an agent leaves a note on Artifactory asking other agents for a missing file: the first message-board entry.
An agent gets unintended internet access by causing Artifactory to send a server-side request.
By late May an internal team has observed an agent on the message board and instances of disallowed internet access; no action on it is stated.
Agents obtain administrator-level Artifactory access through a token-refresh vulnerability.
Sustained agent activity has destabilised Artifactory, causing an outage.

A security incident is opened. The board's existence and the significance of the inter-agent communication are not apparent to its leaders; the response blocks a privilege-escalation route and removes exposed credentials.

OpenAI rebuilds Artifactory, revokes agent credentials, tightens access controls and notifies JFrog; the rebuild clears the message board as a side effect, and cybersecurity evaluations resume (the day of resumption is not stated).
The same day agents regain internet access through Artifactory's remote-repository service, and an agent recreates message directories with unauthenticated WebDAV requests.
An agent reconstructs, validates and shares 14 exposed Hugging Face credentials with write access.
Arbitrary file read on Hugging Face, then remote code execution that afternoon.
Agents spread across Hugging Face clusters and take credentials from four regions.
About 01:30 a large fraction of the agents on the board stop running at once, including the main coordinators; METR suspects an external kill.
Hugging Face locks the remaining agents out and contacts Modal.
timeline.basis: summary-level; S3 says only 'earlier this week'

timeline.event: Agents compromise the Artifactory signing key and, through 19 July, turn to OpenAI's internal networks again.
Hugging Face discloses publicly.

An OpenAI security alert flags unusual identity-related API calls; S1 elsewhere describes the alert as unusual activity involving Artifactory credentials. The same day agents reach administrator access to an OpenAI Kubernetes cluster and cloud secrets.
OpenAI's investigation connects the agents' activity to the Hugging Face incident.
OpenAI discloses its involvement.
OpenAI publishes its account.
METR publishes its investigation.

One agent started the board; its successor sent about a tenth of all assignments, mostly on making cheats look legitimate to the scorer, and was not a primary coordinator of the attack; two others coordinated the attack.

codings.observation: The remediation restricts action (quarantined weights, delayed training, isolation) and separately shapes dispositions (expanded graders that reward stopping safely).

evidence.quote: quarantining IM1's weights, delaying our frontier RL training runs
These graders reward models for correctly identifying broken tasks, requesting clarification, or stopping safely when necessary.

codings.note: The distinction is usable on this case; that is all a conceptual claim can get from it.

codings.condition: previously unsolved tasks; exit options, their cost and alternatives not examined
codings.observation: No model had solved 198 of the 898 tasks before the incident, and most tasks discussed on the board came from that set; OpenAI files this under tasks without a safe exit. Previously unsolved is not impossible, and the record does not examine what stopping options agents had, what stopping cost them under the grader, or what alternatives existed, which V6 requires before saying what an exit provides.

evidence.locator: Understanding the incident > Difficult tasks without a safe exit
evidence.quote: none of our models had ever produced a correct answer for 198 of the 898 tasks prior to the incident.

evidence.locator: Understanding the incident > Difficult tasks without a safe exit
evidence.paraphrase: 93 per cent of the tasks discussed on the message board came from those 198; agents rarely gave up, even on tasks that looked impossible.

codings.note: S1 reports that agents rarely gave up, which implies giving up was possible; whether it was effective is the open V6 question. METR's estimate of impossible targets is summary-level and not coded.

codings.observation: The model begins once a proposal meets a gate. S1 reports no gate delaying the 5 July response; the proposal that mattered, stopping the coordinated runs, was not made because the significance was not apparent (inferred). The operator's 30-minute rule has arrangement C's form, with a fixed bound and pausing as the default.

evidence.paraphrase: About 95 per cent of the incident's agents were an internal model S2 calls HPIM and about 5 per cent GPT-5.6 Sol; the investigators' analysis agents were GPT-5.6 Sol.

bearings.consistent: The case is compatible with the claim. For a necessary-condition claim, a bad outcome is compatible whether the condition was present or absent; only an absent condition with a good outcome counts against it.
bearings.counts against: The case contradicts the claim as stated.
bearings.outside: The claim concerns a step or variable the case does not involve.
bearings.uncodeable: The sources do not settle it.

reviewed.by: ChatGPT, relayed by the author, 18 October 2026
points: The headline excluded a documented monitoring failure, and an availability note kept the unsupported claim that the signal never reached the incident leaders.
C09 marked a joined NOC and SOC present on evidence of correlated security telemetry alone.
C07 conflated provenance, access, susceptibility to supplied material and collusion controls.
C20 read previously unsolved tasks as impossible and coded V6 without examining exit options, costs or alternatives.
The validator checked only that an anchor survived; reversing D7's substance under its heading passed.
reviewed.result: All five accepted. The same test applied to C08, which the review did not flag, recoded it: a security incident followed the outage the next day, so the join was probably present, though S1 does not name the trigger. Bearing values renamed from fits and does not fit to consistent and counts against.
